newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Clinton Australia visit seen as sunny photo-op.
newsitem.headline: Clinton Australia visit seen as sunny photo-op.

text.p: The government is pushing free trade, the media wants action on China, but analysts said on Tuesday they expected little of substance from U.S. President Bill Clinton's visit to Australia.

Clinton is due to spend just one hour in official talks with Prime Minister John Howard and make a speech to parliament before spending two days relaxing at the tropical Barrier Reef resort town of Port Douglas, in northern Queensland state.
In between, a cruise on Sydney's famed harbour and a golf game with world number one Greg Norman are the highlights of the visit, which starts on Tuesday and ends on Saturday.
"This is basically a holiday trip," Australian National University senior lecturer Michael McKinley told Reuters.
"Major issues of foreign policy, or any other major issues are not going to be discussed at great length. This is basically an extraordinary photo-op."

The conservative Liberal-National government, which ended 13 years of Labor rule in a March national election, pledged to reinvigorate links with Washington, a relationship Howard says was neglected by his predecessor, Paul Keating.

McKinley and other analysts say susbtantial progress in boosting ties was achieved at ministerial talks in July, when both countries announced upgraded defence links, a new security pact and a boost in military exercises.

But those talks, Canberra's renewed focus on Washington, a series of diplomatic gaffes and Australia's race debate have angered Beijing and prompted a chill in relations that threatens to make itself felt during the Clinton visit.
"The playing-up of the U.S. alliance has provoked China," Defence Force Academy lecturer Carl Thayer told Reuters.
"The Howard government is sending a most confused signal all across the front. It signals the wrong way for engagement with southeast Asia."

Chinese and Australian ministers have reportedly postponed official visits and the Chinese media have made vocal attacks on Australia, accusing Canberra of pandering to U.S. interests and allying with Washington to contain China.
"When the White House launched an air attack on Iraq, Canberra was unusually eager to ape Uncle Sam at every step," the official China Daily said in a commentary.
"Such parrot-like behaviour can only lead to unpopularity in the international community," the newspaper said.
Leading Australian newspapers and Labor opposition leader Kim Beazley urged Howard to raise the China issue with Clinton.

"Its (China's) perception is that ... Washington is using Japan and Australia as ... anchors of an encirclement of China that represents a potential threat to China's interests in the region," The Australian newspaper said in an editorial.
"This Chinese perception is something that Mr Howard and Mr Clinton need to review comprehensively."
But most analysts expect the issue to be barely touched on.
Both leaders are scheduled to meet Chinese president Jiang Zemin in Manila over the weekend, ahead of Monday's summit of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum leaders.
Howard told Tuesday's The Sydney Morning Herald newspaper he would try to put Sino-Australian relations back on track during his talks with Jiang.
"We obviously have differences on issues, but I just don't think they should be allowed to contaminate our bilateral relationship," he said.
Howard, in a series of media interviews timed for Clinton's visit, said his talks with Clinton would focus heavily on trade.
But analysts expect little progress there, too, ahead of the APEC summit and next month's World Trade Organisation ministerial meeting in Singapore.
